name: The Angels
line: Created from light, they never disobey Allah and carry out what they are commanded.
story: Before Adam was made, Allah told the angels He would place a successor on earth. They asked why, then bowed to Adam when commanded. They have wings, two, three or four, and more. They worship without tiring, night and day. Belief in them is one of the pillars of faith.
lesson: Some of the most constant worshippers of Allah are beings we will never see.
note: The Quran mentions angels about 88 times. Their creation from light is stated in the hadith of Muslim.

name: Jibril
line: The trusted spirit who brought Allah's words down to the prophets, last of all to Muhammad ﷺ.
story: Jibril is called the Trustworthy Spirit and the Holy Spirit in the Quran. He came to Maryam in the form of a man, and to Muhammad ﷺ in the cave of Hira with the first word, Read. He took the Prophet ﷺ on the Night Journey and once came in front of the Companions to teach them Islam, iman and ihsan.
legacy: Every verse of the Quran reached the Prophet ﷺ through him.
when: Brought revelation to the prophets; to Muhammad ﷺ from 610 to 632 CE
note: Named three times in the Quran (2:97, 2:98, 66:4). Most scholars say 'the Spirit' (al-Ruh) in 97:4 and 78:38 is also Jibril.

name: Mikail
line: One of the two angels named together in the Quran, beside Jibril.
story: The Quran names Mikail once, when some of the Jews of Madinah said Jibril was their enemy. Allah answered that whoever is an enemy to Jibril and Mikail is an enemy to Allah. Scholars say he is entrusted with rain and the growing of provision. The Prophet ﷺ named him in his prayer at night.
lesson: The angels are one team under one Lord; you cannot love some and hate others.
note: His charge over rain and provision comes from the commentators and weaker narrations, not from the Quran.

name: Israfil
line: The angel who will blow the Trumpet that ends the world and then raises the dead.
story: The Quran describes the Trumpet blown twice. At the first blast everyone in the heavens and earth falls dead, except whom Allah wills. At the second, all stand up looking on. Tradition names the one who blows it as Israfil, who waits with the Trumpet to his lips for the command.
lesson: The end of the world is one breath away, and only Allah knows when.
note: Israfil is not named in the Quran. The name appears in the Prophet's night prayer (Muslim 770); that he blows the Trumpet comes from other narrations and the commentators.

name: The Angel of Death
line: The angel entrusted with taking every soul when its time comes.
story: The Quran names him only as the Angel of Death, with helpers who take souls with him. For the believer they come gently, with peace. For the wrongdoer they come striking faces and backs. No soul is taken a moment early or late.
lesson: Death has an appointed messenger, and he does not miss an appointment.
when: At every death, from Adam's children to the end
note: The name Azrail is popular but is not found in the Quran or in authentic hadith.

name: Munkar and Nakir
line: Two angels who question each person in the grave about their Lord, religion and prophet.
story: When the dead are buried, two angels come and sit them up. They ask: Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is this man who was sent to you? The believer answers firmly. The Prophet ﷺ linked this moment to the verse about Allah keeping the believers firm with the firm word.
lesson: The answers in the grave are learned by how you live, not memorised at the end.
when: In the grave, after each death
note: The Quran alludes to the questioning; the names Munkar and Nakir come from the hadith in al-Tirmidhi, graded hasan.

name: Kiraman Katibin
line: Two angels with every person, writing down every word and deed.
story: The Quran says there are noble guardians over every person, recording, who know what you do. One sits on the right and one on the left, and not a word is spoken without a watcher ready. On the Day of Judgement each person is handed the book they wrote.
lesson: Every day you are writing your own book.
when: With every person, all their life

name: The Guardian Angels
line: Angels who take turns guarding each person, in front and behind, by Allah's command.
story: Besides the recorders, the Quran speaks of angels who follow one another around each person and protect them by the decree of Allah. Over every soul there is a protector. When the appointed death arrives, the protection is lifted and the messengers of death take over.
lesson: You are guarded far more than you know.
when: With every person, all their life

name: The Bearers of the Throne
line: Mighty angels who carry Allah's Throne and pray for the forgiveness of the believers.
story: The Quran says those who carry the Throne and those around it glorify Allah and ask Him to forgive the believers, to save them from the Fire and to bring their families into Paradise. On the Day of Judgement, eight of them will bear the Throne. The Prophet ﷺ described the vast size of one of them.
lesson: The angels nearest the Throne are praying for ordinary believers.
when: Before creation of humankind, and on the Last Day
note: Whether 'eight' in 69:17 means eight angels or eight ranks is discussed by the commentators.

name: Malik, keeper of the Fire
line: The angel in charge of Hell, who answers the people of the Fire: you will remain.
story: The Quran gives one scene. The people of the Fire call out, O Malik, let your Lord finish us off. He replies that they will stay. He is not cruel; he carries out justice exactly as commanded, and never disobeys.
lesson: There will be no escape to beg for later, so the time to turn back is now.
note: Named once in the Quran. Not to be confused with the scholar Malik ibn Anas.

name: The Keepers of the Fire
line: Stern and severe angels set over Hell; the Quran says there are nineteen.
story: Over Saqar are nineteen, the Quran says, and Allah made their number a test. The disbelievers mocked it, thinking they could overpower nineteen. The keepers are harsh and strong and never disobey. They ask those thrown in: did no warner come to you?
lesson: The Quran's details are sometimes a test of whether we believe or mock.
note: Az-Zabaniyah (96:18) is understood by most commentators as the angels of Hell.

name: Ridwan
line: The name tradition gives to the keeper of Paradise, whose angels greet the believers with peace.
story: When the believers are led to Paradise in groups, its keepers open the gates and say: Peace be upon you, you have done well, enter to stay forever. Angels come in to them from every gate. Later tradition names the chief keeper Ridwan, a word that also means Allah's good pleasure.
lesson: The last greeting a believer hears at the gate is peace.
note: The Quran speaks of the keepers of Paradise but does not name them. The name Ridwan comes from later tradition and weak narrations.

name: Harut and Marut
line: Two named in Babylon who taught magic only after warning: we are a trial, so do not disbelieve.
story: The devils taught people magic in Sulayman's time, and Sulayman never disbelieved. In Babylon, Harut and Marut also taught, but each time warned that they were only a test. People learned from them how to split husband and wife, yet nothing could harm anyone except by Allah's permission.
lesson: Knowledge used to harm is a test, and the harm only happens by Allah's permission.
when: Linked in the Quran to Sulayman's time (date unknown)
note: Most scholars say they were angels sent as a trial. Some read 'malikayn' (two kings) and say they were men. The story of their falling in love with a woman named Zuhra is Isra'iliyyat, rejected by many scholars.

name: The Guests of Ibrahim
line: Angels who came to Ibrahim as guests with news of a son, then went on to destroy Lut's people.
story: They arrived as strangers and said peace. Ibrahim hurried out a roasted calf, but their hands did not reach for it and he grew afraid. They told him not to fear: they were sent to Lut's people, and Sarah would have Ishaq. Then they went to Lut, who did not recognise them either, and saved him by night.
lesson: Generosity to guests is the way of Ibrahim, even when you do not know who they are.
when: In the time of Ibrahim and Lut
note: Some commentators name Jibril, Mikail and Israfil among them; the Quran does not say how many there were.

name: The Angels Who Spoke to Maryam
line: Angels who called Zakariya in his prayer niche and told Maryam she was chosen above the women of the worlds.
story: While Zakariya stood praying in the sanctuary, angels called out that he would have a son named Yahya. They also spoke to Maryam: Allah has chosen you and purified you. Then they gave her news of a word from Allah, whose name would be the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam.
lesson: Allah chooses whom He wills, and the angels announce it.
when: Shortly before the births of Yahya and Isa
note: Many commentators say the 'angels' here means Jibril, using the plural for honour.

name: The Two Disputants of Dawud
line: Two who climbed into Dawud's prayer chamber with a case about ninety-nine ewes and one.
story: Dawud was alarmed when two litigants climbed the wall of his prayer room. One said his brother had ninety-nine ewes and wanted his single one too. Dawud ruled that the brother had wronged him. Then he realised he was being tested, fell down bowing and turned to Allah, who forgave him.
lesson: Even a prophet-king turns to Allah the moment he senses a test.
note: Most commentators say they were two angels in human form; some say they were men. Stories about Dawud and another man's wife are Isra'iliyyat and rejected as unworthy of a prophet.

name: The Angels of Badr
line: Angels sent in ranks to strengthen the believers at Badr and in later battles.
story: At Badr the Muslims were few and begged Allah for help. He answered: I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another. They made the believers firm and struck the enemy. The Quran also mentions unseen soldiers at Hunayn, in the cave of the Hijrah and at the Trench.
lesson: Victory comes only from Allah; the angels are a glad tiding to calm the heart.
when: Badr, 2 AH (624 CE), and later battles

name: The Angels Who Pray for Believers
line: Angels who send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ and ask forgiveness for those on earth.
story: The Quran says Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, and on the believers too, to bring them out of darkness into light. The angels glorify their Lord and ask forgiveness for those on earth. When believers stand firm, angels come down to them saying: do not fear, do not grieve.
lesson: When you send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, you join the angels in what they do.

name: The Angels of the Night of Decree
line: Angels and the Spirit who descend on Laylat al-Qadr with every decree until dawn.
story: The Quran was sent down on a blessed night better than a thousand months. On that night the angels and the Spirit come down by their Lord's permission, with every matter. Every wise affair is made distinct. It is peace until the rising of the dawn.
lesson: One night of worship can outweigh a lifetime, so seek it in the last ten nights of Ramadan.
when: Every year on Laylat al-Qadr, since the Quran was first sent down

name: The Jinn
line: A hidden creation made from smokeless fire, with free will like humans, some believers and some not.
story: Allah created the jinn before Adam, from a smokeless flame of fire, and He created jinn and humans only to worship Him. Like us they can choose: some are righteous and some are not. They can see us where we cannot see them. Iblis was one of them. A whole surah, al-Jinn, carries their words.
lesson: We share this world, and its test, with another creation.

name: The Jinn Who Listened
role: First jinn to hear the Quran
line: A band of jinn heard the Prophet ﷺ recite the Quran, believed, and went home as warners.
story: A small group of jinn came upon the Prophet ﷺ reciting in prayer. They told each other: listen quietly. When it ended they went back to their people and said: we have heard an amazing Quran that guides to the right way, so we believe in it. The Prophet ﷺ only learned of it through revelation.
legacy: Surah al-Jinn records their words, and Muslims count believing jinn as part of the ummah.
note: Many place this at Nakhlah on the way back from Ta'if; Ibn Abbas reports it on the road to Suq Ukaz. Some scholars say there were several such meetings.

name: The Eavesdropping Devils
line: Rebellious jinn who once crept up to steal news from the heavens, now chased off by shooting flames.
story: The jinn used to sit in places in the sky to overhear the angels and pass scraps to soothsayers. When the Prophet ﷺ was sent, they found the heaven filled with strong guards and burning flames. Anyone who listens now finds a flame lying in wait. This is why the soothsayers' news dried up.
lesson: Fortune-tellers trade in stolen scraps mixed with lies.
when: Barred from the heavens when the Prophet ﷺ was sent

name: The Qarin
line: A companion from the jinn assigned to every person, whispering to them all their life.
story: The Quran says whoever turns away from the remembrance of Allah, a devil is assigned as his companion. On the Day of Judgement that companion will disown him: I did not make him transgress. The Prophet ﷺ said every person has a qarin from the jinn, and that Allah helped him against his, so it only told him good.
lesson: Remembering Allah is the guard against the whisperer who never leaves.
when: With every person, all their life
note: In Surah Qaf, many commentators take the companion of 50:23 to be the recording angel, and the one of 50:27 to be the devil.

name: The Jinn of Sulayman
line: Jinn put to work for Sulayman, building palaces and statues, diving for pearls, and fearing to stop.
story: Allah gave Sulayman command over the jinn. They built what he wished: high chambers, statues, basins like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons, and dived into the sea. When he died leaning on his staff, they kept working, until a creature of the earth gnawed the staff and he fell. Then the jinn realised they never knew the unseen.
lesson: Even the jinn do not know the unseen; only Allah does.

name: The Ifrit of Sulayman
line: A mighty jinn who offered to fetch the Queen of Saba's throne before Sulayman rose from his seat.
story: Sulayman asked who would bring him Bilqis's throne before she came to him in submission. An ifrit from the jinn said he could do it before Sulayman stood up from his place, and that he was strong and trustworthy. But a man with knowledge of the Book offered to do it in the blink of an eye, and did.
lesson: Knowledge from Allah outran the strength of the jinn.

name: The Hur al-Ayn
line: Pure companions of Paradise, likened in the Quran to hidden pearls and guarded rubies.
story: The Quran promises the people of Paradise pure companions with lovely eyes, like pearls kept hidden, untouched before by any human or jinn. They are a reward for what the believers used to do. Scholars add that the righteous women of this world will be even more beautiful in Paradise than the hur.
lesson: Whatever we give up for Allah here, He replaces with better.

name: The Youths of Paradise
line: Ever-young servants who circulate in Paradise with cups and pitchers, like scattered pearls.
story: The Quran describes youths made eternal, going round among the people of Paradise with cups, jugs and a drink from a flowing spring that brings no headache. When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls. They serve, and those they serve are honoured.
lesson: In Paradise the believer, who served others here, is served.
note: Scholars differ on who they are: a special creation of Paradise, or, in one view, children who died young.

name: The Beast of the Earth
line: A creature Allah will bring out of the earth near the end, speaking to people that they did not believe.
story: When the word comes due against people, Allah will bring out for them a creature from the earth that speaks to them, because people were not certain of Allah's signs. The Prophet ﷺ listed it among the ten major signs before the Hour, with the sun rising from the west.
lesson: There comes a time when signs no longer help, so believe while belief still counts.
note: Its appearance and place of emergence are described in narrations of mixed strength; the Quran gives only this verse.
